Peripheral nerves connect the central nervous system (CNS) with tissues, such as bone, joints,
muscles, tendons, and skin.
Nerves that supply the musculoskeletal system provide motor and sensory function.

Function
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is composed of 42 pairs of nerves that exist outside
of the brain and spinal cord, including cranial nerves (except cranial nerve II); spinal
nerves; and the roots, branches, and nerves that extend from them as they travel to
their end-target muscle or organ. The PNS provides motor innervation to muscles and
relays sensory information from specialized receptors to the CNS. The constant
communication between the central and peripheral nervous systems via sensory input
and motor output allow for complex coordinated movements and fine motor control of
the musculoskeletal system. The nerves also carry postganglionic autonomic control
fibers, which regulate various physiologic functions of the body.
Neuron Anatomy
Every neuron contains a cell body, which is its metabolic center.
The cell bodies of most neurons also give rise to one long branch, known as an axon, which is
the primary distal projection, and to several short branches, known as dendrites, which are
thin nerve processes that receive input from other nerves (Figure 1).
Myelin, which is composed of lipids and proteins from the cell membranes of specialized glial
cells called Schwann cells, forms an insulating sheath around the axons of neurons in the
PNS. One function of myelin is to speed the conduction of action potentials along the axons
of nerve cells.
As an axon reaches its end organ, it divides into fine terminal branches with specialized
endings called presynaptic terminals, which are responsible for transmitting a signal to
postsynaptic receptors.

Figure 1 Illustration shows a neuron, which is the smallest functional unit of peripheral nerves.
The dendrites receive information (afferent) and the axon transmits information (efferent) to
other neurons or to end organs such as motor end plates. The axon hillock is the site where
the axon originates from the cell body. Each axon is covered by a cellular sheath, otherwise
known as the axolemma. Myelinated nerve fibers have axons that are surrounded by a series
of Schwann cells, each wrapped around the axon many times to form the myelin sheath. The
segments of axon between Schwann cells are called nodes of Ranvier. Axons can form
branches at the nodes of Ranvier, allowing a single cell body to innervate multiple end organs.

Neuron Anatomy
Neurons are the cells that make up nervous tissue and are the smallest functional unit of
nerves. They consist of a cell body or soma, an axon, and multiple dendrites. The soma
contains the nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, ribosomes, neurofilaments,
Nissl bodies, and lysosomes that serve critical functions in neuronal activity, metabolism,
and production of proteins and structures required for signal transmission and
neurotransmitter release. Dendritic processes receive signals from other cells and the
environment and transmit this information to the soma in an afferent pathway. The
axon is a long cytoplasmic extension that communicates signals as action potentials in
an efferent direction from its somatic origin known as the axon hillock. The axon of a
neuron meets the dendrites of one or more adjoining neurons at a junction called the
synapse, the location at which action potentials from the axon stimulate the release of
neurotransmitters from vesicles at the nerve terminal. Neurotransmitters passively cross
the synapse and bind to receptors on the membranes of the dendrites of the
postsynaptic neurons. The dendrites then convey the transduced information to the cell
body so that it can be processed.1 The cell membrane of the axon is specialized for
signal conduction and is referred to as the axolemma. Within the axolemma is the
axoplasm, which contains organelles and structures to support its function and serves as
a conduit for transport of substances to and from the axon terminal.
Sensory neurons are pseudounipolar, with a long axon extending in both directions
(centrifugally and toward the CNS) with a cell body that resides in the dorsal root
ganglion. Motor neurons of the PNS (lower motor neurons) have cell bodies that
originate in the anterior horn of the spinal cord (CNS) and extend along their path to
terminate at a specialized synapse called the neuromuscular junction (NMJ).
Schwann cells are a type of glial cell that envelop the axons of peripheral nerves and
provide vital support for the development, maintenance, and regeneration of neurons.

In larger neurons, Schwann cells also form a myelin sheath along the axolemma by
wrapping their plasma membrane around the axon multiple times, which provides
insulation and aids in the efficient propagation of action potentials along the axon.
Nerve Anatomy
Nerve fibers are collections of axons with Schwann cell sheaths.
Afferent nerve fibers convey information from sensory receptors to the CNS.
Efferent nerve fibers transmit signals from the CNS to muscle and other tissues in the
periphery of the body (ie,, outside the brain and the spinal cord).
Nerve fibers are classified based on their size and conduction velocity (Table 1).

A nerve fiber consists of a neuron and its Schwann cells. Typically, myelinated nerve
fibers are large in diameter (>2 to 20 μm) and have many circumferentially wrapped
Schwann cells in series along the entire length of the axon (Figure 2). Myelinated
segments of axon are called internodes, and the spaces between the sheaths are termed
nodes of Ranvier. The nodes of Ranvier are approximately 1 μm in length and are spaced
out by the internodes approximately 1 mm apart; however, the size of each may vary
with the size and type of nerve fiber.
Figure 2 Illustrations show the formation of the myelin sheath as the Schwann cell wraps
around the axon multiple times, as seen in sequential illustrations 1 through 4. (Modified
with permission from Kuczynski K: Functional micro-anatomy of the peripheral nerve
trunks. Hand 1974;6[1]:1-10.)
Within the nodes of Ranvier are high concentrations of voltage-gated Na+ and K+ ion
channels, which function in action potential propagation in a process called salutatory
conduction, as the signal jumps from node to node, which speeds up conduction along
myelinated nerve fibers. Schwann cells that support unmyelinated nerve fibers surround
multiple axons in a group to provide support to the cell without creating the multilayered
myelin sheath (Figure 3). They typically are 0.2 to 3 μm in diameter, and conduction is
slower along the unmyelinated axons.
Large myelinated nerve fibers, such as those of motor nerves, have the fastest
conduction velocity and are classified as group A nerve fibers (Aa). Medium and small
myelinated sensory nerve fibers belong to other subclasses of group A, termed Aß and
Ad, and are composed of sensory nerves carrying signals, such as cutaneous touch and
pressure and pain and temperature, respectively. Group B nerve fibers include small

Composition
A nerve consists of collections of nerve fibers called fascicles and of neural connective tissue,
which surrounds and lies within each fascicle (Figure 4).
The axons within a fascicle are surrounded by a connective tissue layer called endoneurium.
Perineurium is a thin, dense connective tissue layer that surrounds the fascicles of a nerve.
Epineurium is a supportive sheath that contains multiple groups of fascicles. It also contains a
well-developed network of extrinsic, interconnected blood vessels that run parallel to the
fascicles.
The structural organization of fascicles changes throughout the length of a nerve. As fascicular
plexuses unite and divide within a nerve, the number and size of fascicles change.

Composition
Nerves are made up of multiple nerve fibers bundled together and giving off branches of
nerve fibers as they travel toward their target end organs. Most peripheral nerves
contain a mixture of myelinated and unmyelinated fibers and may be purely motor,
sensory, or both (most common). The nerve fibers are held together by the connective
tissues of the endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium, which provide structural
support and protection and help maintain the environment to support nerve health and
function2 (Figure 5).

The endoneurium is the innermost layer, surrounding each nerve and its Schwann cells.
Endoneurium is primarily composed of a collagenous matrix with fibroblasts, mast cells,
and capillaries and forms a bilaminar sheath around the axon, Schwann cells, and myelin
of a nerve fiber.1 The perineurium bundles nerve fibers into fascicles and helps form the
blood-nerve barrier. It has a high tensile strength and maintains interfascicular pressure,
providing a barrier to perineurial diffusion. This barrier limits injury to nerve fibers by
limiting diffusion of the epineurial edema fluid that occurs in stretch and compression
injuries. The barrier created by the perineurium also limits the diffusion of endoneurial
edema fluid that can occur if a nerve is compressed.1 The epineurium is a protective
layer around the entire nerve formed by the collection of groups of fascicles. The

perineurium and epineurium are thicker across joints and at the location at which the
nerve is under stress. These layers are continuous with the meninges of the CNS.
Fascicles do not run as isolated, parallel strands from the spinal cord to a presynaptic
terminal or end organ. The structural organization of fascicles changes throughout the
length of a nerve as fascicular plexuses unite and divide within a nerve. At the joint level,
the fascicles of a nerve are numerous and are smaller to accommodate nerve
deformation as the joint goes through a range of motion. For example, the ulnar nerve
at the elbow contains many small fascicles, which minimize injury to this nerve with
elbow flexion and extension. In contrast to the ulnar nerve, the radial nerve at the level
of the spiral groove has a small number of large fascicles, which do not tolerate stretch
well. This level-specific internal anatomy places the radial nerve at greater risk for
neurapraxia if it is mobilized and retracted from the spiral groove.1
Blood Supply
A peripheral nerve has intrinsic and extrinsic vessels, with multiple anastomoses between one
another throughout the length of the nerve.
At the epineural level, no blood-nerve barrier exists.
At the capillary level within the endoneurium, a blood-nerve barrier, similar to the blood-
brain barrier, exists. This barrier prevents the diffusion of various macromolecules into the
nerve, maintaining neural integrity. The blood-nerve diffusion barrier can be damaged by
infection, radiation, or metabolic disease.

Blood Supply
Nerves are supplied by a rich anastomotic network of extraneural and intraneural blood
flow that supports healthy nerve activity and metabolism by supplying oxygen and
nutrients and removing waste products. The extrinsic neural blood supply comes from
many segmental arteries in series along the length of the nerve, which travel through the
mesoneurium (a loose layer of areolar tissue external to the epineurium) and form the
vasa nervorum, entering the epineurium and anastomosing with adjacent segmental

circulation and the interfascicular networks of the intrinsic system in the perineurial and
endoneurial spaces. A dense network of endoneurial capillaries from the intrinsic system
supply the innermost nerve fibers of fascicles, whereas the most superficial are more
dependent on extrinsic supply from the segmental arteries. Because of the distribution
of vascular flow, centrally located fascicles are more susceptible to vascular disorders
and ischemia. The vessels of the extrinsic system are coiled to allow for mobility of the
system with nerve stretching and excursion without compromising blood flow.2,3 This
vessel architecture, along with the segmental nature, makes the blood supply relatively
resistant to damage or mobilization of short segments of the nerve. Intrinsic vessels are
protected by the connective tissues layers of the perineurium and endonerium and glide
with the nerve fibers during nerve mobilization. Despite the protective biomechanical
properties, these vascular networks are quite easily disrupted in patients who sustain
trauma, patients with compression, and patients with other insults to the nerve.2 The
blood-nerve barrier is formed by endothelial cells from the endoneurial capillaries and
those of the internal zone of the perineurium, which are joined together by tight
junctions to prevent passage of macromolecules and maintain nerve homeostasis by
regulating a hypertonic environment and a positive fluid pressure within endoneurial
spaces (2 to 3 mm Hg).3 The electrochemical concentrations are important for the
proper conduction of action potentials along the nerve, and the positive hydrostatic
pressure helps prevent intraneural swelling and edema.1-3

Nerve Endings
Several types of sensory nerve endings exist, each specialized for a particular type of
sensory input. A sensory signal must be transduced by these receptors into an electrical
signal to be transmitted by the nerve fiber. Ion channels open in response to mechanical
pressure, temperature, and noxious or other stimuli to stimulate and transmit the signal.
The intensity of the stimulus is related to the frequency of the action potentials
generated. Adaptation is the decrease in signal intensity (frequency of action potentials)
with repeated stimuli of the same type at a receptor. Receptors may be rapidly or slowly
adapting depending on their sensory function. The cutaneous area that a single neuron
innervates is called the receptive field. Areas with highly sensitive tactile discrimination,
such as the fingertips and hands, are innervated by large numbers of neurons with small
receptive fields.
Nonencapsulated receptors are made up of free nerve endings of sensory axons and
typically register noxious and painful stimuli (nociceptors) and thermal stimuli
(thermoreceptors). Encapsulated receptors include Meissner corpuscles, Merkel disk
receptors, Pacinian corpuscles, and Ruffini endings. Tactile mechanoreceptors are
specialized to detect pressure, vibration, position, and other physical stimuli. Superficial
cutaneous mechanoreceptors include Meissner corpuscles, which are rapidly adapting
receptors that are sensitive to moving tactile stimulation, and Merkel disks, which are
slowly adapting and sense constant pressure, texture, and low-frequency vibrations.
Static and moving two-point discrimination can be used to evaluate the innervation
density of Merkel cells and Meissner corpuscles, respectively.2,4,5 Semmes-Weiss
monofilaments can be used to assess the touch threshold by Merkel cells.
Mechanoreceptors located in the subcutaneous tissues consist of Pacinian corpuscles,
which detect high-frequency vibration and are quickly adapting, and Ruffini corpuscles,
which slowly adapt and detect sustained pressure and stretching of the skin. Tuning
forks can be used to test the vibration threshold of Pacinian corpuscles.

Muscle spindles are intramuscular mechanoreceptors that sense muscle stretch. They
innervate groups of specialized intrafusal muscle fibers and are part of the myotatic
reflex arc. Stretch of the muscle spindle and contraction of intrafusal fibers activate the
muscle spindle, and the body responds by stimulating contraction of the muscle fibers
via gamma motor neurons. In the myotatic reflex, coordination of synergistic muscle
contraction and/or inhibition of antagonistic muscles sometimes occurs to provide a
precise motor response. Golgi tendon organs are proprioceptive organs that detect
muscle tension and are located at myotendinous junctions. They provide inhibitory
signals to muscles that contract too tightly to prevent excess tension and damage to the
tendons.
Nerve Metabolism
Axoplasmic transport is possible via polarization of the neuron.
Proteins, which are created only in the cell body of a neuron, travel via antegrade transport
through the axon and dendrites of the neuron to support neural functions, such as action
potential propagation and neurotransmitter release.
Degradation products travel back to the cell body via retrograde transport. Several other
factors also travel to the cell body in retrograde fashion, including nerve-growth factors (NGFs),
some viruses (eg, herpes simplex, rabies, polio), tetanus toxin, and horseradish peroxidase
(used in the laboratory to identify the location of a cell body in a dorsal root ganglion or in the
spinal cord).

Nerve Metabolism
Axonal transport occurs along microtubules that are oriented in a polarized fashion
(positive end towards the axon terminal) within the axon and allow for antegrade
transport of substances created in the soma to the axon terminal to support growth and
metabolic activity and retrograde transport of materials from the environment and
substances to be recycled or discarded, which also helps the cell regulate protein
synthesis. Vesicular transport to the nerve terminals also delivers neurotransmitters and
other vital signaling molecules to the axon terminal. Slow axonal transport carries

Embryology of the Nervous System
The nervous system (and skin) is formed by the ectoderm, which, with the mesoderm and
endoderm, is one of the three germ layers of embryonic tissue.
The ectoderm divides to form the neural tube, which gives rise to the brain, spinal cord, and
motor neurons; the neural crest, which evolves into afferent neurons; and the epidermal layer
of the skin.
The PNS is divided into the autonomic nervous system, a purely motor visceral system, and a
mixed sensory and motor somatic system, which helps control voluntary motion.

Embryology of the Nervous System
Neurulation begins during the third week of development; the neural plate forms from
thickened columnar epithelium on the dorsal surface of the embryo. The inner portion
of the neural plate forms the CNS, whereas the outer portion of the neural plate forms
the PNS. Trophic signals from the mesoderm underlying the neural plate stimulate
formation of the neural groove, which deepens and becomes enclosed by the fusion of
neural folds on each side, forming the neural tube and crest at approximately
gestational day 18.4 The CNS develops from the neural tube. Neural crest cells are
multipotent; they migrate to the periphery and become neurons and glial cells that make
up the PNS. Neural crest cells also give rise to melanocytes, smooth muscle, craniofacial
structures, and adrenal glands, among other cells and tissues.
Axonal growth and development are initially guided by various NGFs.
N-cadherin and neural cell adhesion molecule are adhesive membrane
glycoproteins that are expressed on neural ectoderm and help guide growing axons.

Laminin and fibronectin are glycoproteins of the extracellular matrix that promote
the directional growth of nerve fibers.
Other factors thought to enhance nerve regeneration include NGF, fibroblast growth
factor, ciliary neuronotrophic factor, and insulin-like growth factor.
The neural tube forms the spinal cord. Neural crest cells migrate to the periphery and
develop into neurons and glial cells, forming sensory ganglia in the dorsal root ganglia,
autonomic ganglia, and neural plexuses. Neuroblasts migrate along radial glia, which
provide a pathway along which the neurons grow. A neural growth cone forms at the
terminal end of the axon and is the site of continued growth as the axon develops
towards its target destination, guided by Schwann cells, neurotrophic factors, and other
chemoattractant signals. A complex balance of stimulatory and attractant signals and
repulsive and inhibitory signals assists in driving the axon along its intended pathway. As
development continues, the Schwann cells, connective tissue sheaths, and other
supporting cells take their place along the nerve fibers and lead to additional
differentiation and development of axons into mature nerve fibers. As the central and
peripheral nervous systems continue to mature during the postnatal and postpartum
period, myelination and neural connections become more robust (especially throughout
the first 2 years of life), and pruning of weak or erroneous connections ensures discrete
and strong neural communication. Similar processes govern nerve regeneration after
peripheral nerve injury (PNI).1,4
Spinal Nerves
Spinal nerves are collections of axons that exit the spinal cord at distinct levels (8 cervical, 12
thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal).
The efferent ventral root of a spinal nerve transmits information from the brain to muscle; the
afferent dorsal root carries signals from the periphery back to the CNS.
Spinal nerves frequently collect into plexuses (cervical, brachial, lumbar) before branching.

Spinal Nerves

Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves exit the spinal cord at distinct levels (8 cervical, 12
thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal), leaving the vertebral column through the
intervertebral foramina.1 Spinal nerves have proximal branches that form the ventral
and dorsal roots. Convergence of the roots form the spinal nerves, which communicate
information between the spinal cord and the rest of the body and vice versa. The
efferent ventral root of a spinal nerve transmits information from the brain to muscle;
the afferent dorsal root carries signals from the periphery back to the CNS.1 Fibers of the
sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the autonomic nervous system also are
part of the spinal nerves and the innervate glands, smooth muscle, and visceral organs.
Cell bodies of efferent motor nerves are located in the anterior horn of the spinal cord
and, therefore, are within the CNS.1 Sensory afferent nerves have cell bodies located in
the dorsal root ganglion just lateral to the entry point of the dorsal root into the spinal
cord. As spinal nerves exit the cord, they divide into anterior and posterior rami.
Posterior rami supply innervation to muscles and joints of the spine, posterior trunk, and
skin of the back, whereas anterior rami supply the anterior and lateral trunk and give
rise to nerves of the extremities. Distal to the nerve root, spinal nerves become
peripheral nerves and frequently collect into plexuses (except in the thoracic region)
before branching and traveling to their targets.1 Each afferent spinal nerve receives
sensory information from a discrete area of skin known as a dermatome. Although
dermatomal innervation is specific for a spinal nerve, overlap of sensation from adjacent
nerve roots is present for each dermatome. Therefore, complete sensory loss is not
detectable unless two or more contiguous nerves have been affected, except in a few
areas in which this overlap does not occur. These include the lateral arm and the
proximal lateral forearm supplied by C5, parts of the thumb and the index finger
supplied by C6, the long and lateral index fingers supplied by C7, the little finger and the
distal hypothenar region supplied by C8, the medial part of the leg supplied by L4, the
dorsum of foot and the great toe supplied by L5, and the lateral foot supplied by S1.
Knowledge of these autonomous zones of innervation is important in assessing damage
to nerves of each of these roots via physical examination.3,6,7

Disorders of Myelination
Demyelination may result from auto-immune, metabolic, and hereditary disorders;
infection; ischemia; compression; and toxins (eg, medications, alcohol). Multiple
sclerosis, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), and Guillain-Barré
syndrome (GBS) are examples of nervous system diseases that cause demyelination and
slowed nerve-conduction velocities. Multiple sclerosis affects the CNS and is a chronic
(relapsing and remitting) neurologic disorder characterized by the perivascular
infiltration of inflammatory cells followed by damage to the myelin sheaths of nerves
and to nerve fibers themselves. Problems with motor control (eg, vision, strength,
balance) and cognition occur in patients with multiple sclerosis.1 CIDP is an autoimmune
demyelinating disorder similar to multiple sclerosis that affects the PNS. GBS is an acute,
inflammatory condition affecting nerves and spinal nerve roots (ie, a
polyradiculoneuropathy). GBS is presumed to be an autoimmune condition, typically
triggered by a viral or bacterial infection that causes the production of antibodies that
attack the myelin sheath. The loss of myelin leads to an acute impairment of sensory and

Nerve Conduction and Biomechanics
Nerve Conduction
Propagation of a nerve signal
The axon membrane of a neuron consists of a selectively permeable lipid bilayer that
contains gated ion channels and transmembrane pumps, which are necessary to maintain
the resting membrane potential that allows for signal transmission.
Conduction of signals along an axon begins with action potentials, which are generated if the
axon membrane is depolarized beyond a critical threshold.
The rate at which an action potential is conducted along an axon depends on the size of the
axon and the presence of myelin; larger axons and myelinated axons carry action potentials
more rapidly than smaller or unmyelinated axons.
Within the nodes of Ranvier, dense collections of voltage-gated sodium channels propagate
the action potential, allowing saltatory (pulse-like) conduction between one node and the next.
Motor nerve signals terminate at the NMJ. This is a highly specialized region between the distal
nerve terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber, the location at which the signal is transduced to
stimulate muscle contraction or relaxation.

Nerve Conduction
The resting membrane potential of a neuron (ie, the relative difference in charges across
the cell membrane at rest) is approximately -70 mV. This potential is maintained by
several pumps and ion channels, which help maintain a higher concentration of Na+ and
Cl- ions in the extracellular fluid and K+ in the intracellular space, which is responsible for
the negative resting potential that exists within the axon membrane.1,2 These pumps
derive their energy from sodium/potassium adenosine triphosphatase, which cleaves a
phosphate bond from adenosine triphosphate to form adenosine diphosphate, releasing
energy to actively transport 3 Na+ ions out of the cell, and 2 K+ ions into the cell against
their concentration gradients. The control of gated ion channels (Na+ and K+) is primarily
governed by electrical (voltage-gated), chemical (ligand-gated), and mechanical
(mechanical-gated) stimuli. If a stimulus causes the Na+ ion channels to open, Na+ flows
rapidly into the axon via passive transport because of the high electrochemical gradient,
causing the cell to depolarize as the Na+ enters and increases the membrane potential.1

Nerves are viscoelastic structures that respond to stress in a nonlinear manner.

Neurapraxia is an immediate, localized blocking of neural conduction, with normal

Axonotmesis involves axon disruption without the destruction of Schwann cells,

Neurotmesis is complete disruption of a nerve.
No spontaneous recovery of the affected nerve can be expected.
Mechanisms of injury include open crush, violent stretch, and laceration.

Compression
If a nerve is compressed, nerve fibers are deformed, local ischemia occurs, and
vascular permeability is increased.
Edema then affects the endoneurial environment, resulting in poor axonal
transport and nerve dysfunction.
If compression continues, the edema and dysfunction persist, and fibroblasts
invade the nerve, producing scar tissue, which impairs the gliding of nerve fascicles
over one another in joint flexion.
Tissue pressures as high as 30 mm Hg can result in paresthesias and increase the
latency of nerve conduction. A tissue pressure of 60 mm Hg can completely block
nerve conduction.

After 15 minutes of anoxia, axonal transport stops.

transmission are lost within the first 48 to 96 hours. As Wallerian degeneration proceeds,

regeneration. Chromatolysis occurs in the cell body as metabolism is reprogrammed to
form proteins, lipids, and other necessary structures for cellular repair. Schwann cells
divide and form cytoplasmic processes called Bünger bands that line up along the
original basement membrane associated with Schwann cells of the myelin sheath. This
forms the scaffolding upon which axonal regeneration will occur and guide the axon to

With or without suture re-approximation of disrupted nerve ends, nerve
regeneration begins with axonal elongation across the zone of injury (Figure 7).
The zone of injury undergoes an ingrowth of both capillaries and Schwann cells.
The Schwann cells migrate from the proximal and distal stumps of a disrupted

columns (bands of Bünger) to guide the tip or growth cone of the axon or fiber.
The growth cone is sensitive to neurotrophic growth factors, such as NGF, and

Distal reinnervation of muscle occurs only if the muscle has viable motor end plates
that a regenerating nerve can stimulate.
In the acute period after a nerve injury, muscle innervated by the injured nerve
increases the number of its motor end plates, seeking stimulation by the nerve.
With the occurrence and continuation of fibrosis, the number of motor end plates
diminishes.

injury to the motor nerve that serves it.

Diagnostic Studies
Overview
The primary tests used to evaluate the integrity of the PNS are EMG and NCS.
These tests assess the function of sensory nerves, motor nerves, and muscles to confirm
diagnoses of neuropathies and myopathies.
They also can differentiate causes of weakness, identify the level and severity of nerve
injuries or abnormalities of conduction, and demonstrate the existence of denervated
muscle and its reinnervation.
NCS (Figure 8)
Sensory nerve function
The signal produced by stimulation of a mixed (motor and sensory) nerve is called a
compound nerve action potential.
A signal specifically related to the sensory function of a nerve is called a sensory nerve
action potential.
Nerve conduction velocity (distance/time) or latency (time between the stimulus that
induces an action potential and the onset of the potential) typically is recorded (Figure 8).
Typically, nerve conduction velocity is decreased and latency is increased by temperature,
age, demyelination, and loss of axons because these factors decrease the rate of impulse
transmission through nerves.
The amplitude of a sensory nerve action potential also can be measured. Reductions in
temperature increase sensory nerve action potential amplitude; increasing age decreases
sensory nerve action potential amplitude.

EMG
EMG studies cover an entire motor unit (eg, anterior horn cell of the spinal cord, motor
neuron, and muscle) and involve measuring insertional activity, which is the activity of a
muscle if the needle electrode of an electromyograph is inserted into it; spontaneous
activity of the muscle; motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) of the muscle, which are
characterized by their duration, amplitude, and shape; and recruitment, which is the
successive activation of additional motor units upon stimulation of a single motor unit.
These studies do not measure or assess sensory information.
Insertional activity is measured as the needle electrode is passed into the muscle belly.
Decreased insertional activity results from poor muscle viability, muscle fibrosis, or
muscle atrophy.
Increased insertional activity may be a sign of denervation or a primary muscle disorder
(eg, polymyositis, myopathy).
Spontaneous activity involves electrical discharges in muscle that occur without muscle
contraction and without movement of the testing needle.
Fibrillations are an example of abnormal spontaneous activity; they occur in denervated
muscle fibers and in some myopathies. The density of fibrillations is graded from 1+ to 4+,
but it is their amplitude that helps in understanding the time of occurrence of denervation of
a muscle.
Large-amplitude fibrillations frequently occur acutely (within 3 to 12 months after
denervation), and smaller amplitude fibrillations occur later in the process of denervation
(after the muscle has atrophied).
Positive sharp waves are abnormal electrical discharges of single muscle fibers that can be
seen in association with fibrillations. They also can be seen without fibrillations if a muscle

MRI
MRI may be a useful adjunct to electrodiagnostic studies for assessing various disorders of
the PNS.
MRI may show changes in muscle from denervation. For example, chronic denervation will
show evidence of fatty atrophy.
High-resolution images with sufficient contrast are necessary to emphasize peripheral nerve
anatomy and nerve morphology.
The studies that provide these images take advantage of differences in the MRI signal of
distinct intraneural tissues, resulting from differences in the water content and physical
structure of fascicles, perineurium, and epineurium.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is being used more commonly in the diagnosis and evaluation of PNI and
brachial plexus injury if superficial enough for quality imaging.
Ultrasonography is user-dependent and visualization of some neural anatomy often is
difficult secondary to depth and scar tissue that develops after injury.
Advantages of ultrasonography are that it can show anatomic and morphologic
characteristics of lesions; it is cheap and readily available; and it can be used for therapeutic
purposes, such as diagnostic and therapeutic nerve blocks.

Diagnostic Studies
Electrodiagnostic studies, including NCS and EMG, are best thought of as an extension of
the patient history and physical examination. They are useful in assessing the extent of
injury and recovery and for surgical decision making. NCS evaluate the nerve fibers,
including axonal fibers and myelin integrity and the functionality of the nerve fiber. EMG
assesses electrical activity of muscle. Electrodiagnostic studies may cause considerable
patient discomfort, which may lead to incomplete tests, thereby affecting the diagnostic
sensitivity. Regardless, they are very helpful to the clinician in characterizing injury
severity, location, prognosis, and monitoring recovery over time. An intimate
understanding of the normal anatomy and pathoanatomy of nerves is essential in
analyzing electrodiagnostic test results. In NCS, latency and nerve conduction velocity
reflect transmission of nerves and correlate with axonal injuries causing demyelination.
The nerve being examined in a conduction velocity study can be stimulated in an
antidromic (antegrade) manner, in which the nerve impulse travels in a proximal-to-
distal direction, or in an orthodromic (retrograde) manner, in which the nerve impulse
travels in a distal-to-proximal direction. Quantification of the speed of conduction of an
action potential requires knowledge of the distance (in millimeters) across which the
action potential travels and the time (in milliseconds) required for it to travel across that
distance.1 Amplitude, also measured by NCS, reflects quantity of functioning nerve
fibers. EMG evaluates target end muscles innervated by specific nerves at rest and
during voluntary contraction and, therefore, requires patient participation. Anatomic
and functional understanding are paramount for performing the test accurately. Needle
EMG interrogates a single neuromuscular unit. Sequential testing at various locations
within a single muscle may increase sensitivity (Figure 10). Spontaneous depolarization
activity of a muscle is observed if motor innervation is lost (fibrillations and positive
sharp waves). Because of the temporal range of Wallerian degeneration, EMG will not
appear abnormal for 10 to 14 days; however, it is not typically performed until 3 to 4
weeks postinjury. Absent MUAPs in the activation phase represent neurotmetic injuries,
and they are proportionally decreased in advancing degrees of axonotmetic injuries.
Muscle recruitment also may characterize the degree of injury, with decreased
recruitment correlating with more severe denervation after PNI. EMG also can determine
if a muscle is receptive to re-innervation or if options, such as tendon transfer, will be
more appropriate to restore function because of low or absent potential for recovery of

Peripheral Nerve Pharmacology
Local anesthetic agents
These agents create a sensorimotor nerve block, causing transient numbness and
paralysis by temporarily disrupting the transmission of action potentials along
axons.
Lidocaine, mepivacaine, and bupivacaine (amide-type agents) have different
durations of action based on their specific biochemistries, with lidocaine having the
shortest duration of action and bupivacaine having the longest duration of action.
C-nerve fibers (eg, cutaneous pain fibers) are the most susceptible to the effects of
local anesthetic agents, and A-fibers (eg, motor axons and deep pressure sense) are
the least susceptible to the effects of local anesthetic agents.
Local anesthetic agents of the amide type are processed by the liver via cytochrome
P450 enzyme into metabolites that are more water soluble than their parent
compounds; these metabolites are then excreted in the urine.
Epinephrine may be combined with these anesthetic agents for vasoconstriction.
This combination reduces the systemic absorption of local anesthetic agents from
the injection site by decreasing blood flow in the area around the site.
Local anesthetic agents work as antagonists to fast Na+ ion channels, preventing
membrane depolarization and, therefore, inhibiting the ability of the nerve to generate
action potentials. Local anesthetic agents may be combined with epinephrine to reduce

Botulinum toxin
Botulinum toxin, produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, may be injected
into muscle to manage muscular spasticity.
If used to manage muscle spasticity, the beneficial effect of botulinum toxin begins
approximately 7 to 14 days after injection and typically lasts 3 months.
Botulinum toxin works at the level of the NMJ. If injected into muscle, it blocks the
release of acetylcholine from axon terminals at the presynaptic clefts of the NMJ,
preventing acetylcholine from reaching the motor end plate and triggering muscle
contraction. Therefore, it causes chemical denervation and muscle paralysis.1 This is
referred to as a type A neuromuscular blockade. The cumulative maximum
recommended dose to manage muscle spasticity is 400 units in a 3-month period, with
